messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: include files in builds?
parts:
Has anyone given any thought to how we can extend the Stan
language with the equivalent of a pre-processor? There are
integration issues with the way we build models. And we
want whatever we do to work in RStan and PyStan, too.

Option 1:

Literally have include statements in the Stan language.

1a. Implement with fancy iterator specialization directly in
the parser. (May be more efficient, but if we need efficiency
here, we're probably in big big trouble when it comes time to
compile.)

2a. Implement as a preprocessor, generating a single input
string, then parsing it. (Much easier.)

An issue is how to specify paths and coordinate that with the
call to stanc. Ben suggested something like the "-I" convention
used in C++. I like the idea of following C++ conventions.


Option 2:

Have some way to include one or more library files of function
definitions from the stanc call. Ideally, these would be compiled
separately and linked somehow rather than being continually rebuilt.
But this is tricky as we need the signatures from their declarations
in order to validate the rest of the parse. We aren't putting errors
off until link time!

An issue is getting things into the right namespace, but I can just
add a namespace for all the user-defined functions and include it, and
similarly for system-defined functions.


Global Issue:

I've realized since playing with functions a bit that you can't
really modularize the construction of a model because the variables
all still need to be declared in the data and parameters block.

It might be nice to have a way to define a whole submodel that
adds in its data and parameters to another model's. Good thing
I didn't use the terminology "submodel" for void functions :-)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: include files in builds?
parts:
On Wednesday, April 23, 2014 7:02:54 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Has anyone given any thought to how we can extend the Stan
language with the equivalent of a pre-processor?  There are
integration issues with the way we build models.  And we
want whatever we do to work in RStan and PyStan, too.

Option 1:  

Literally have include statements in the Stan language.

1a.  Implement with fancy iterator specialization directly in
     the parser.  (May be more efficient, but if we need efficiency
     here, we're probably in big big trouble when it comes time to
     compile.)

2a.  Implement as a preprocessor, generating a single input
     string, then parsing it.  (Much easier.)

An issue is how to specify paths and coordinate that with the
call to stanc.  Ben suggested something like the "-I" convention
used in C++.  I like the idea of following C++ conventions.

Not sure about 1a vs 2a or why 2a isn't 1b but I think -I will be easy to understand. Particularly if the path is
  • Whatever additional directories are specified by -I
  • The directory where the model is build
  • Some directory in the stan tree
then, the user wouldn't have to actually specify -I very much. Also, it might be nice that if foo is declared but not defined, then stanc would look on the include path for a foo.stan file with the definition(s).

Option 2:

Have some way to include one or more library files of function
definitions from the stanc call.  Ideally, these would be compiled
separately and linked somehow rather than being continually rebuilt.
But this is tricky as we need the signatures from their declarations
in order to validate the rest of the parse.  We aren't putting errors
off until link time!

An issue is getting things into the right namespace, but I can just
add a namespace for all the user-defined functions and include it, and
similarly for system-defined functions.
Sounds fine, but I don't know if this is something that could replace 1.

Global Issue:

I've realized since playing with functions a bit that you can't
really modularize the construction of a model because the variables
all still need to be declared in the data and parameters block.

It might be nice to have a way to define a whole submodel that
adds in its data and parameters to another model's.  Good thing
I didn't use the terminology "submodel" for void functions :-)

This would be good for multilevel models particularly with ragged data structures. I was thinking about using this for a model with the 51 states, where I basically have a function that does the log-posterior contribution for a state and then pass the data and parameters to it. But then I have to do

data {
  int<lower=51,upper=51> S;
  int<lower=1> N[S];
  int<lower=1> K[S];
  matrix[N[1],K[1]] x_AL;
  matrix[N[2],K[2]] x_AK;
  ...
  matrix[N[51],K[51]] x_WY;
}

and similarly for parameters. It would be nice if I could pass 51 localized submodels and yet somehow have them recognize some global parameters.

Ben

parts:

> On Wednesday, April 23, 2014 7:02:54 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

I wasn't very clear. I was trying to contrast a simple preprocessor which
produces a sequence of bytes as output with something more complicated that
could precompile whole bits of a model. And we'd probably want to do both.
I'm thinking the preprocessor would be a standalone function (callable
from command line for CmdStan) that would expand the input into a big
string and then parse it. I'm thinking option 2 is the much more complicated
independent compiler and linker.

> but I think -I will be easy to understand. Particularly if the path is
> • Whatever additional directories are specified by -I
> • The directory where the model is build
> • Some directory in the stan tree
> then, the user wouldn't have to actually specify -I very much. Also, it might be nice that if foo is declared but not defined, then stanc would look on the include path for a foo.stan file with the definition(s).
>
> Option 2:
>
> Have some way to include one or more library files of function
> definitions from the stanc call. Ideally, these would be compiled
> separately and linked somehow rather than being continually rebuilt.
> But this is tricky as we need the signatures from their declarations
> in order to validate the rest of the parse. We aren't putting errors
> off until link time!
>
> An issue is getting things into the right namespace, but I can just
> add a namespace for all the user-defined functions and include it, and
> similarly for system-defined functions.
>
> Sounds fine, but I don't know if this is something that could replace 1.

Yes you'd probably want to do both. If there was a way to get the names
in, you could replace 1 just by separately compiling and then linking,
rather than putting everything together to compile.

>
> Global Issue:
>
> I've realized since playing with functions a bit that you can't
> really modularize the construction of a model because the variables
> all still need to be declared in the data and parameters block.
>
> It might be nice to have a way to define a whole submodel that
> adds in its data and parameters to another model's. Good thing
> I didn't use the terminology "submodel" for void functions :-)
>
> This would be good for multilevel models particularly with ragged data structures. I was thinking about using this for a model with the 51 states, where I basically have a function that does the log-posterior contribution for a state and then pass the data and parameters to it. But then I have to do
>
> data {
> int<lower=51,upper=51> S;
> int<lower=1> N[S];
> int<lower=1> K[S];
> matrix[N[1],K[1]] x_AL;
> matrix[N[2],K[2]] x_AK;
> ...
> matrix[N[51],K[51]] x_WY;
> }
>
> and similarly for parameters. It would be nice if I could pass 51 localized submodels and yet somehow have them recognize some global parameters.
>

I'd like to see is this:

matrix[N,K] x[51];

Then x is a size 51 array where x[s] is an N[s] by K[s] matrix.
The underlying model code would all support this because arrays
are just std::vector and the sizes aren't part of the type for
dynamic Eigen matrices.

We'd want to allow either dimension to be an int or an array
of ints, and if they're arrays, their sizes would have to match.

It's a pretty big project, but doable.

A related thing I'd like to do is this:

real L[N];
real U[N];
real<lower=L,upper=U> x[N];

which would declare x to be a size N array of real values,
each with a separate constraint. Same vectorization concerns
for L and U.

A third related issue is indexing, where I want to allow
an array of indexes instead of an index and have it produce
an array of the values at those indexes. Basically, the way
it works in R is this:

> a = (1:4)^2
> a[c(2,4)]
[1] 4 16

So you could write a varying slope and intercept model like this:

int<lower=1> I; // number of groups
real alpha[I]; // varying slope
real beta[I]; // varying intercept

int<lower=0> N; // number of data points
real x[N]; // predictors
real y[N]; // outcomes
int<lower=1,upper=I> ii[N]; // group indicators

The indexing would be defined so that alpha[ii] is an array of size N, defined
so that

alpha[ii][n] == alpha[ii[n]].

So the model looks like this:

y ~ normal(beta[ii] + x .* alpha[ii], sigma);

There are a lot of places where this would reduce looping.
In general, I think we'd want to allow an array to be indexed
by an array of integers and return an array of that size with
the associated values.

We could also write a polymorphic compose function instead, which
is really what's going on here with the notation alpha[ii]. It'd
look like this in terms of signatures:

T[] compose(T[], int[])

where T is any legal Stan type, and it'd be defined so that

compose(x,ii)[n] = x[ii[n]]

- Bob
